comments: Smoke test: cross-compilation target flag parsing and codegen dispatch.
The Mach-O (write_macho_x86 / write_macho_arm64) and PE/COFF (write_pe) backends
were implemented but previously undocumented as "not yet wired".  They are in fact
dispatched by the codegen driver in main() based on TARGET_OS / TARGET_ARCH:
--target x86_64-linux   → TARGET_OS=0, TARGET_ARCH=0 → write_elf()       (default)
--target aarch64-linux  → TARGET_OS=0, TARGET_ARCH=1 → write_elf_arm64()
--target x86_64-macos   → TARGET_OS=2, TARGET_ARCH=0 → write_macho_x86()
--target aarch64-macos  → TARGET_OS=2, TARGET_ARCH=1 → write_macho_arm64()
--target x86_64-windows → TARGET_OS=3, TARGET_ARCH=0 → write_pe()
This file is a minimal Sounio program that compiles and runs correctly on Linux
(the host platform).  The cross-compilation targets require running the produced
binary on the corresponding OS; the compiler itself will emit a valid Mach-O or
PE/COFF file when invoked with the appropriate --target flag.
To manually verify cross-compile flag acceptance:
$SOUC compile tests/run-pass/cross_compile_flag.sio -o /tmp/out.macho --target x86_64-macos
$SOUC compile tests/run-pass/cross_compile_flag.sio -o /tmp/out.pe    --target x86_64-windows
Both commands should succeed with exit code 0 and emit the respective binary format.

description: PR #2515 review round 5 (review 5300804681), findings A (comment_id 4090734423, self-hosted/check/specializer.sio) and B (comment_id 4090734484, self-hosted/ir/lower.sio): the `use`-tracking registries this
comments: PR #2515 review round 5 (review 5300804681), findings A (comment_id
4090734423, self-hosted/check/specializer.sio) and B (comment_id
4090734484, self-hosted/ir/lower.sio): the `use`-tracking registries this
PR built (SPEC_USE_MODULE_HASH, LOWER_USE_MODULE_HASH, and
CHECKER_USE_MODULE_HASH) recorded EVERY segment of a `use` path as a
module name, including the terminal segment of a path-form NAMED import
like `use a::b::specific_fn;` -- where `specific_fn` is the actual
imported FUNCTION, not a module. `use epistemic::propagate::monte_carlo;`
is exactly this shape (a real import, see
tests/stdlib/epistemic/test_stiff_ode_knightian_mc.sio:33):
`monte_carlo` is a function in stdlib/epistemic/propagate.sio, not a
module. Recording it as a known module let `monte_carlo::tc_c_add(..)`
(a bogus qualified path through a nonexistent "monte_carlo" module) get
silently treated as valid -- checker_path_qualifier_all_modules_known
returned true for the qualifier, so the checker bound the call to the
REAL (unrelated) `tc_c_add`'s signature instead of rejecting the
nonsensical namespace with W044.
The AST cannot distinguish a path-form named-item import's terminal from
a genuine whole-module import's terminal (both are `use_glob=false,
use_items=None, seg_count>=2`), so all three registries still record
every segment. The fix instead lives in module_frontend.sio's import-file
resolution (resolve_import_file_path and its raw-scanner sibling): when
the full `use` path does NOT resolve as a file but dropping its last
segment DOES, that is the authoritative, file-resolution-backed answer
that the last segment names something inside the parent file, not a
module of its own -- recorded via lower_named_item_terminal_note
(parser/ast.sio's AST_NAMED_ITEM_TERMINAL_* registry) and read back by
check.sio / lower.sio / specializer.sio's own qualifier-trust checks
(lower_named_item_terminal_known) instead of each guessing from an
incidental name collision with some unrelated top-level function
elsewhere in the program (an earlier, unsound heuristic tried and
reverted in round 6). `monte_carlo` resolves this way, so
`monte_carlo::tc_c_add(..)` now falls back to the pre-existing
"unresolved path" W044 warning instead of being silently accepted.
Round 12 (review comment 4106485575): this used to be a `//@ compile-fail`
fixture pinning `//@ error-pattern: W044` -- but W044 is intentionally a
non-fatal warning (the whole point: the call still compiles and evaluates
to 0 rather than being hard-rejected), so it could never by ITSELF make
`souc compile` exit non-zero. The original call, `monte_carlo::tc_c_add(2,
3)`, only made the fixture "pass" because the SAME fallback quirk this
finding documents -- treating the qualifier's bare first segment as the
callee, ignoring `tc_c_add` entirely -- then type-checked `(2, 3)` against
`monte_carlo`'s OWN 3-parameter signature (Epistemic, fn(f64)->f64, i64)
and additionally rejected the missing Prob/Div effects, producing
E009/E010/E035 on top of W044. Fixing that unrelated quirk later could
make the file compile cleanly even with W044 correctly still firing,
silently turning this into a vacuous pass. Fixed by matching the call's
argument list and the caller's effects to `monte_carlo`'s real signature
exactly, so nothing else can fire: `souc check` now exits 0 with W044 as
the ONLY diagnostic, and `//@ check-only` + `//@ expect-stdout-contains`
pin exactly that -- decoupled from whether the fallback quirk itself ever
gets fixed.

The signed domain gave Sub an escape hatch: a non-disjoint pair is ALLOWED
when ns_cov_nonneg proves every shared source carries a non-negative
coefficient product. That certificate is only as good as the signs feeding
it, and the transfer originally sent every operator except Sub, Mul and Div
through ns_union -- the ADDITIVE join. OpRem landed there. So
r = a % b        published a's and b's additive signs as if they were r's
s = r - a        found `a` at + in both operands, certified Cov >= 0,
and COMPILED
but Rem's Jacobian signs are not the additive join of its operands' signs, so
that certificate was unfounded and Var(r - a) could be understated -- the
exact thing E230 exists to refuse, reintroduced through the new escape hatch
rather than through the rule it guards.
The fix makes ns_union_opaque the DEFAULT and ns_union the exception (OpAdd
only): an operator nobody has modelled marks its result sign-unknown, and
ns_cov_nonneg fails closed on it. This file must stay refused. If it ever
compiles again, the transfer has gone back to trusting signs it cannot derive.

- has_shadow == true  (left_sshadow = 0 >= 0)

The pattern used to read E001, which this program never emits — it is rejected
by the refinement checker with an uncoded diagnostic. The harness was not
matching error-pattern at all, so the test passed while asserting the wrong
thing; with the matcher fixed the annotation had to say what is actually
emitted.
`requires: lean_single` because the diagnostic this asserts is an engine
difference, not a language rule. Measured 2026-09-03 on both:
lean_single  error[E208]: refinement type violation — value 0 does not
satisfy parameter predicate at line 19        ← what is asserted
Madaros      error[E008] return value does not match declared return type
error[E001] this binding expects a different type
error[E009] argument type does not match parameter
Madaros is not missing the diagnostic — check.sio carries code 42, "value does
not satisfy the refinement predicate". It never reaches it, because it relates
a refinement type to its base type in NEITHER direction:
fn f(x: Positive) -> i32 { x }    E008, though every Positive IS an i32
let p: Positive = 0               E001, a bare type mismatch standing where
the predicate should have spoken
So the three errors above are all one gap wearing three codes, and the E009 at
the call site rejects for the wrong reason: NonNeg and Positive differ as
NAMES, not because 0 fails `n > 0`. Two identical refinement names with a
violated predicate would slip through it.
Erasure (Positive → i32) would be sound to open on its own. The introduction
direction is where the predicate must actually be evaluated, and opening it
without first proving the check fires would turn a wrongly-coded rejection
into an acceptance — a fail-open in a type system. Left for whoever implements
refinement subsumption in the modular checker, rather than half-done here.
